'''George Irving Bell''' (August 4, 1926 &ndash; May 28, 2000) was an American [[physicist]],<ref>{{cite journal|author=Perelson, Alan S.|author2=Goldstein, Byron|title=Obituary: George Irving Bell|journal=Physics Today|date=April 2001|volume=54|issue=4|pages=85–86|doi=10.1063/1.1372123|bibcode = 2001PhT....54d..85P |doi-access=free}}</ref> [[biologist]], and [[mountaineering|mountaineer]], and a grandson of [[John Joseph Seerley]].<ref>[http://wc.rootsweb.ancestry.com/cgi-bin/igm.cgi?op=DESC&db=geolarson2&id=I187556 Descendants of John Seerley], George Larson II, 2010-07-04</ref> He died in 2000 from complications of [[leukemia]] after surgery.<ref name="nyt">"George Irving Bell, 73, Leader In Studies of Genome" (obituary), ''New York Times'', June 18, 2000, Section 1, p. 32.</ref>

==Education==
Bell received a [[bachelor's degree]] in physics from [[Harvard University]] in 1947. He studied [[theoretical physics]] with [[Hans Bethe]] at [[Cornell University]], obtaining his doctorate in 1951.<ref name="lanl">[http://www.lanl.gov/orgs/pa/News/060800text.html Los Alamos National Lab News]</ref>

==Physics==
Immediately after receiving his Ph.D., Bell went to the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory]] and joined the "T Division." At the time, this division was primarily occupied in the design of the first [[thermonuclear weapon]]. Bell contributed by solving problems of [[neutron]] transport.<ref name="lanl"/>

Such problems are also crucial in the design and analysis of [[nuclear reactor]]s, so it was natural that Bell became a leading expert on the physics of reactors. He co-authored the book ''Nuclear Reactor Theory''<ref name="nrt">''Nuclear Reactor Theory'', Robert E. Krieger Publishing, 1985. See [http://www.rpi.edu/~danony/PhysNucRea/PNROutline.htm Physics of Nuclear Reactors] at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute|RPI]]</ref> with [[Samuel Glasstone]].<ref name="lanl"/>

==Biology==
Bell's interests turned to biology in the 1960s, creating quantitative models in [[immunology]]. He headed the Theoretical Biology and Biophysics group at Los Alamos from 1974 to 1990.<ref name="lanl"/> He also worked on mathematical models in biophysics.<ref name="nyt"/> In 1988, he became the founding director of the Center for Human Genome Studies, which became a major participant in the [[Human Genome Project]]. He was director for only one year (simultaneously acting as the head of T Division and the group leader for the Theoretical Biology and Biophysics group) and retired from Los Alamos in 1990.<ref name="nyt"/> He continued to work as an associate of the laboratory until September 1999.<ref name="lanl"/>

Bell was the author of over 100 research papers and the co-editor of ''Theoretical Immunology'' (1978) and ''Computers and DNA'' (1989; {{ISBN|0-201-51505-9}}).<ref name="nyt"/>

==Mountaineering==
Bell was an avid and accomplished mountaineer and participated in some of the most notable American expeditions of the 1950s and 1960s. His first climbs were during his high school years, in the [[Teton Range|Tetons]], and he was an active participant in the Harvard Mountaineering Club. In the 1940s, he made first ascents of four peaks in the area around [[Mount Waddington]] in the [[Coast Mountains|Coast Range]] of [[British Columbia]], on an HMC expedition. During this period, he also climbed in the Tetons, the [[Wind River Range]], and the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]].<ref name="aajo">[http://www.americanalpineclub.org/AAJO/pdfs/2001/448_inmemoriam_aaj2001.pdf In Memoriam section] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927212552/http://www.americanalpineclub.org/AAJO/pdfs/2001/448_inmemoriam_aaj2001.pdf |date=September 27, 2007 }} of the ''[[American Alpine Journal]]'', 2001</ref>

Bell then moved to more significant objectives, organizing the expedition in 1950 that made the first ascent of [[Yerupajá]], 21,769 feet (6,635 m), in the [[Cordillera Huayhuash|Huayhuash]] mountain range of [[Peru]], one of the most difficult and dangerous peaks in the [[Andes]]. Bell did not make the summit but reached an altitude of 20,600 ft (6,300 m). He returned to Peru in 1952 to make the first ascent of another steep and difficult peak of the Peruvian Andes, [[Salcantay]] in the [[Vilcabamba mountain range]]. He made two significant return trips to Peru in 1954 and 1956.<ref name="aajo"/>

Bell also climbed in the [[Karakoram]] of [[Pakistan]], participating in two very notable expeditions. In 1953, Bell took part in the [[Third American Karakoram Expedition]] to [[K2]] and was one of five climbers who fell during a failed attempt of the first ascent of the peak.  Their fall was arrested by [[Pete Schoening]] in one of the greatest feats of mountaineering.  Bell went on several more Himalayan expeditions and made the first ascent of [[Masherbrum]], the 22nd highest peak in the world, in 1960.<ref name="aajo"/>

Bell's son, also named George, is also a climber.
